title: Can Your Help Desk Run the New Estate?
say: Welcome. This briefing comes from Book 15 of the Federal Modernization Workbook, Compliance Automation and Day-Two Operations. It's written for CIOs, service desk and operations leads, and information system security officers. I'll take four questions. Why does modernization succeed or fail at the help desk? What does day two run on? Who runs it? And how do you run it, and prove it works? The short version is this. Cutover proves the new estate can be built. The first locked-out user on Monday morning proves whether it can be run. Let's start with why the help desk holds the keys.

title: The help desk holds the keys
say: Modernization programs spend most of their attention on day one: the tenant is built, identities sync, the cutover runs. But the estate is judged on day two, when every reset, unlock and new hire lands at the help desk. In Entra ID the help desk's power is real. Microsoft calls the Helpdesk Administrator role privileged, and warns that changing a user's password can mean taking over that user's identity. Forcing MFA re-registration wipes the user's methods, and whoever registers next controls the account. So a reset on an unverified request isn't a support task. It's handing the account to whoever asked. Attackers know this; CISA has described groups that talked help desk staff into exactly that. And when the governed path is hard, the desk works around it. Next, what federal guidance says about recovery.

title: Federal guidance treats recovery as a bypass
say: Two federal documents frame the reset and recovery path. OMB's zero trust memo requires phishing-resistant MFA, and then names the hole: recovery is a potential bypass of all that, and a serious threat if it isn't handled. It asks for high-friction methods that are costly for an attacker, like in-person checks or live video. NIST's digital identity guidelines give recovery its own section. They allow a help desk agent only on the basis of a documented risk analysis, repeated proofing has to match the original, and every recovery must notify the account holder. Put together, the help desk reset should be the exception, not the main path, at least as strong as the original proofing, and always followed by a notice. Email, caller ID and knowledge questions verify no one. Now look at the same problem from the compliance side.

title: Compliance decays a click at a time
say: An authorization describes the system as it was assessed. The day after, the help desk resets passwords, onboards people, changes groups and fixes a sync error, and every one of those changes touches a control. Done as portal clicks, they leave no record the control recognizes, so the package ages with every click. The baseline only asks for automation in specific places, so Book 15's push for automation is really about volume. At day-two volume, people assembling the record by hand can't keep up, and what they produce is a reconstruction, not evidence. So a control has three layers: designed, deployed as code, and operated, with an owner, a gate, a clock and an evidence feed. Every operation should start from the source of truth, carry its approval, close with proof and emit its evidence. Miss one, and the work can't be attested. Let's look at the front door.

title: One front door, triage by authority
say: Day two starts at the front door, and the rule is that nothing is handled as ad hoc email to the cloud services team. Self-service requests, the team mailbox, the governance platform and monitoring alerts all land in one triage queue in the service management platform. The mailbox rule has to redirect, not copy, or you end up with two queues. Triage then asks one question: what authority does this task need? The book sorts requests into classes, from no access change at all, through changes the requester's manager approves, up to governance actions like admin consent, which are never automated. The checks run in a fixed order, so the dangerous cases get caught first, such as anything claiming to come from Microsoft, or a target holding a directory role. And an approval nobody answers expires to reject, never to approve. Next, roles.

title: Least-privileged roles, and verify before acting
say: In Entra ID, what a technician can do depends on three things: the role decides the action, the target decides whether it applies, and the administrative unit narrows who it applies to. The program gives each task its least-privileged role, and keeps the role that can reset privileged administrators outside the desk entirely. But capability isn't authority. Some built-in roles can do far more than the task needs, so the program narrows them, sometimes with a custom role. Executives sit in restricted units the general desk can't reach, and roles are eligible through PIM, not standing. And approval isn't identity verification. The verification ladder is the CISO's decision: a phishing-resistant sign-in first, and identity proofing when every method is lost. Then a short-lived one-time pass, a notice on a separate channel, and two approvers for high-risk tasks. Now, the catalog.

title: Catalogs and SaaS: typed requests, verdict first
say: Every routine change arrives as a typed request. The help desk catalog covers joiners, movers, leavers, credentials, groups, licenses, guests and a few more, each tied to the control it exercises and the approval that control needs. And each item closes only when a read of the target confirms the change. The leaver fails audits most often, because it means disabling the account, revoking sessions, deprovisioning every connected app, and reassigning what the person owned. SaaS integration is the riskiest moment. In GCC, an administrator can federate a third-party service in about fifteen minutes, and nothing in that path asks whether the service is authorized to hold federal data. So the catalog records a FedRAMP Marketplace verdict before anything is configured, with Class C or higher as the default for identity data. Next, the inventory everything routes to.

title: The CMDB is a reconciled projection
say: Every ticket names an asset, so the help desk can only be as right as the inventory it routes to. The configuration database earns that trust by agreeing with one authoritative identity, not by being one. Discovery fills it in; the naming and addressing record governs identity. Where the two disagree, the database is wrong, and the disagreement is a finding. ServiceNow already prevents duplicates and controls which source writes each attribute. The program adds one pass: match each asset to the naming record, bind it, and flag the rest, either a shadow asset nobody approved or a gap to fix at the source. Duplicates are resolved by binding, not deleting, so no open finding loses its asset. Otherwise a fix can land on one copy while the finding stays open on the other. Next, automating the controls in each cloud.

title: Control automation per cloud, and the gaps
say: Microsoft, AWS and VMware already ship tools that test most of the settings an assessor asks about. The gap is turning each failed test into owned work with a clock, and each closed task into a record. So the program runs one loop everywhere: the native tool tests, drift is detected, a task is raised, the owning team fixes it, and the task closes on a re-test, not a click. The service management platform reads control state; it never writes it. But the government clouds differ, and several tools are missing, still rolling out, or being retired. The one with a firm deadline is AWS's ServiceNow connector, which loses support on March 31, 2027. The slide lists the rest. And on premises, the agency produces every piece of evidence itself. Before building anything, look at what ServiceNow already does.

title: Native ServiceNow capabilities first
say: Before anyone builds a compliance application, know what the platform already does. ServiceNow's native compliance applications schedule control tests, turn gaps into issues, walk the steps of the Risk Management Framework, give one view of every plan of action, and exchange security plans and assessment results in OSCAL. The government offering is listed as FedRAMP Certified at High. So the recommendation is to buy the native applications first, and build only what they don't do: join every finding to the authoritative asset identity, close only with proof, flag human-only closures, and check the platform's control set against the control map. The principle underneath is this: a control is proven by system evidence wherever a system can see it, and people attest only to what no system can observe. Next, who decides, and who holds the keyboard.

title: One decider per row, and nobody holding the keyboard
say: Day two is run by the people who touch the estate most and decide the least. So every decision sits with someone who isn't holding the keyboard, and every artifact has one owner and a review date. The service desk takes every request, classifies it, verifies the person and executes against an approved ticket. Cloud services is the escalation tier, not a second queue. Technicians approve nothing, and a supervisor never approves a ticket they execute. Platform owners own the runbooks. The control owner owns the approval gate. The service management team builds both and decides neither; changing an approval rule is itself a change the change board authorizes. The board authorizes changes but doesn't accept risk; that goes to the CISO or the authorizing official. A contracted desk fits, because contractors prepare and execute while government officials decide. Now, the runbook.

title: The runbook, and harnesses that check the automation
say: The runbook turns all of this into a rhythm, and each step says what it proves. Daily, a read-only sync probe replaces the habit of logging on to the sync servers each morning, every error becomes a task, and a check confirms every log source is still sending. Weekly, detection rules are tested against replayed known-bad events, and any task closed without proof is either evidenced or reopened. Monthly and quarterly reviews follow, and the slide lists them. The runbook also rewrites everyday tasks. A reset password goes out on a channel separate from the request. And a requester's script is never pasted and run: parameters travel, commands don't. Finally, harnesses check the automation itself. The catch is that a harness that stops running looks just like one that passes, so check that each one ran. That brings us to the decisions.

title: Decisions to make, and next steps
say: So, four decisions. Put identity verification under the CISO, and treat every authenticator reset as an account transfer, with the most friction on the most sensitive accounts and an alert on every reset. Build one front door: redirect the team mailbox, triage by authority, and let unanswered approvals expire to reject. Buy the platform's native compliance applications first, record an authorization verdict before any SaaS integration, and check every feature in your own cloud. And fund the third layer: an owner, a gate, a clock and an evidence feed for every control. The next step needs no procurement. Measure before you build, with a read-only inventory and sync probe in a test tenant, and plan the move off AWS's ServiceNow connector before March 31, 2027. Operations is where modernization becomes routine or quietly reverts. Book 15 has the detail, every claim footnoted. Thank you.
